solution:
The domain is \([3,9]\). Factorise the numerator: \(x^2-3x-10=(x-5)(x+2)\), so for every \(x \ne 5\) in the domain \(f(x)=x+2\), which is a polynomial and hence continuous. In particular the two branches \(3 \le x \le 6\) and \(6 < x \le 9\) carry the SAME expression, so the split at \(x=6\) causes no break: \(\lim_{x \to 6}f(x)=8=f(6)\).
At \(x=5\): \(\lim_{x \to 5}f(x)=\lim_{x \to 5}(x+2)=7\), but \(f(5)=10\). The limit exists and is finite, yet it differs from the value, so \(f\) has a removable discontinuity at \(x=5\).
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is continuous on its domain except at \(x=5\), where the discontinuity is removable.

Each branch is continuous on the interior of its own interval (polynomials, and rational functions whose denominators \(1-x\) and \(x-5\) do not vanish there — note \(1-x \ne 0\) since \(x>2\)). So only the junctions \(x=2,\ x=4\) and the special point \(x=5\) need checking.
At \(x=2\): \(f(2)=2(4)-2(2)+5=9\) and \(\lim_{x \to 2^{+}}\frac{1-3x-x^2}{1-x}=\frac{1-6-4}{1-2}=\frac{-9}{-1}=9\). Continuous.
At \(x=4\): \(\lim_{x \to 4^{-}}\frac{1-3x-x^2}{1-x}=\frac{1-12-16}{-3}=9\) and \(f(4)=\frac{16-25}{4-5}=9\). Continuous.
At \(x=5\): \(\frac{x^2-25}{x-5}=x+5\) for \(x \ne 5\), so \(\lim_{x \to 5}f(x)=10\), while \(f(5)=7\). The limit exists but is not equal to the value, so the discontinuity at \(x=5\) is removable.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is continuous on its domain \([0,7]\) except at \(x=5\).

Use \(\cos C-\cos D=2\sin\left(\frac{C+D}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{D-C}{2}\right)\) and \(1-\cos x=2\sin^2\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\):
\(f(x)=\frac{2\sin\left(\frac{13x}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{5x}{2}\right)}{2\sin^2\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}\).
Divide numerator and denominator by \(x^2\) and use \(\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\sin t}{t}=1\):
\(\lim_{x \to 0}f(x)=\frac{\left(\frac{13}{2}\right)\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}=\frac{\frac{65}{4}}{\frac{1}{4}}=65\).
The limit exists and equals \(65\), but \(f(0)=\frac{68}{15}\ne 65\). The value does not match the limit, so \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x=0\) (a removable discontinuity, removed by redefining \(f(0)=65\)).
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x=0\).

First the value: at \(x=1\), \(\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=1\) and \(\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0\), so \(f(1)=\frac{\pi^2(1)}{3+0}=\frac{\pi^2}{3}\).
Now the limit. Put \(t=1-x\), so \(t \to 0\) as \(x \to 1\), and \(\sin \pi x=\sin(\pi-\pi t)=\sin \pi t\). Hence
\(\lim_{x \to 1}\frac{\sin^2 \pi x}{3(1-x)^2}=\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{\sin^2 \pi t}{3t^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{3}\lim_{t \to 0}\left(\frac{\sin \pi t}{\pi t}\right)^2=\frac{\pi^2}{3}\).
The limit exists and equals \(f(1)\).
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is continuous at \(x=1\).

Factorise: \(2x^2+x-1=(2x-1)(x+1)\), so \(f(x)=\frac{|x+1|}{(2x-1)(x+1)}\) for \(x \ne -1\).
For \(x>-1\): \(|x+1|=x+1\), so \(f(x)=\frac{1}{2x-1}\) and \(\lim_{x \to -1^{+}}f(x)=\frac{1}{-3}=-\frac{1}{3}\).
For \(x<-1\): \(|x+1|=-(x+1)\), so \(f(x)=\frac{-1}{2x-1}\) and \(\lim_{x \to -1^{-}}f(x)=\frac{-1}{-3}=\frac{1}{3}\).
The one-sided limits are unequal, so \(\lim_{x \to -1}f(x)\) does not exist — the second condition for continuity fails.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x=-1\), and it is a jump (irremovable) discontinuity with jump \(\frac{1}{3}-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)=\frac{2}{3}\).

\(f(x)=[x+1]\) is a step function; it can break only where \(x+1\) is an integer, i.e. where \(x\) is an integer. In \([-2,2)\) these are \(x=-2,-1,0,1\).
At an interior integer \(x=c\) (\(c=-1,0,1\)): \(\lim_{x \to c^{-}}[x+1]=c\) while \(\lim_{x \to c^{+}}[x+1]=c+1=f(c)\). The one-sided limits differ, so the limit does not exist and \(f\) is discontinuous there (a jump of \(1\)).
At \(x=-2\), the left endpoint, only right-continuity is required: \(\lim_{x \to -2^{+}}[x+1]=-1=f(-2)\), so \(f\) is continuous at \(x=-2\). On every interval between consecutive integers \(f\) is constant, hence continuous.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x=-1,\ 0,\ 1\) and continuous elsewhere on \([-2,2)\).

\(|x-3| \ge 2\) means \(x-3 \ge 2\) or \(x-3 \le -2\), i.e. \(x \ge 5\) or \(x \le 1\). So
\(f(x)=2x^2+x+1\) on \((-\infty,1] \cup [5,\infty)\) and \(f(x)=x^2+3\) on \((1,5)\). Both pieces are polynomials, so only \(x=1\) and \(x=5\) need checking.
At \(x=1\): \(f(1)=2+1+1=4\), \(\lim_{x \to 1^{-}}(2x^2+x+1)=4\), \(\lim_{x \to 1^{+}}(x^2+3)=4\). Continuous.
At \(x=5\): \(\lim_{x \to 5^{-}}(x^2+3)=28\), but \(\lim_{x \to 5^{+}}(2x^2+x+1)=56=f(5)\). The one-sided limits differ, so the limit does not exist.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\) except at \(x=5\), where it has a jump discontinuity.

The domain is \([-5,-2) \cup (-2,5]\); note \(x=-2\) is excluded. Each branch is a polynomial, so the only possible break is at \(x=-2\).
\(\lim_{x \to -2^{-}}(x^2+x-3)=4-2-3=-1\) and \(\lim_{x \to -2^{+}}(x^2-5)=4-5=-1\).
The two one-sided limits agree, so \(\lim_{x \to -2}f(x)=-1\) exists; the failure is only that \(f(-2)\) is not defined. Defining \(f(-2)=-1\) makes \(f\) continuous on \([-5,5]\).
\(\therefore\) \(f\) has a removable discontinuity at \(x=-2\).

Both branches are polynomials, so the only possible break is at \(x=3\).
\(\lim_{x \to 3^{-}}(x^2+5x+1)=9+15+1=25=f(3)\).
\(\lim_{x \to 3^{+}}(x^3+x+5)=27+3+5=35\).
The one-sided limits are unequal (both finite), so \(\lim_{x \to 3}f(x)\) does not exist and no redefinition of \(f(3)\) can repair it.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x=3\), with jump \(35-25=10\).

On \([0,3)\) the denominator \(x+1 \ne 0\), and on \([3,6]\) the denominator \(x^2-5=0\) only at \(x=\pm\sqrt{5}\approx \pm 2.24\), neither of which lies in \([3,6]\). So each branch is continuous on its own interval and only \(x=3\) needs checking.
\(\lim_{x \to 3^{-}}\frac{x^2+x+1}{x+1}=\frac{9+3+1}{4}=\frac{13}{4}\).
\(f(3)=\lim_{x \to 3^{+}}\frac{3x+4}{x^2-5}=\frac{9+4}{9-5}=\frac{13}{4}\).
Both one-sided limits equal the value \(\frac{13}{4}\).
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is continuous on \([0,6]\); there is no discontinuity.

Factorise both parts: \(x^2-6x+8=(x-2)(x-4)\) and \(x^2-x-12=(x-4)(x+3)\). So
\(f(x)=\frac{(x+3)(x-2)(x-4)}{(x-4)(x+3)}=x-2\) for all \(x \ne -3,\ 4\).
At \(x=-3\) and \(x=4\) the function is not defined (denominator zero), but the limits exist:
\(\lim_{x \to -3}f(x)=-3-2=-5\) and \(\lim_{x \to 4}f(x)=4-2=2\).
Since each limit exists finitely and only the value is missing, both discontinuities are removable. Redefining
\(f(x)=\frac{(x+3)(x^2-6x+8)}{x^2-x-12}\) for \(x \ne -3,4\); \(f(-3)=-5\); \(f(4)=2\)
makes \(f\) continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\).
\(\therefore\) \(f\) has removable discontinuities at \(x=-3\) and \(x=4\), removed by \(f(-3)=-5\) and \(f(4)=2\).

Both branches are polynomials, so the only possible break is at \(x=3\).
\(\lim_{x \to 3^{-}}(x^2+2x+5)=9+6+5=20=f(3)\).
\(\lim_{x \to 3^{+}}(x^3-2x^2-5)=27-18-5=4\).
The one-sided limits are finite but unequal, so \(\lim_{x \to 3}f(x)\) does not exist. A discontinuity is removable only when the limit exists, so no choice of \(f(3)\) can repair this one.
\(\therefore\) \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x=3\); it is a jump discontinuity and is irremovable.

At \(x=2\) the base is \(\frac{10-8}{8-6}=1\) and the index \(\frac{3}{2x-4} \to \infty\), so this is the \(1^\infty\) form; use \(\lim (1+u)^{1/u}=e\).
Write the base as \(1+u\), where \(u=\frac{5x-8}{8-3x}-1=\frac{5x-8-8+3x}{8-3x}=\frac{8(x-2)}{8-3x}\).
Then \(f(x)=(1+u)^{\frac{1}{u} \cdot u \cdot \frac{3}{2x-4}}\), and
\(u \cdot \frac{3}{2(x-2)}=\frac{8(x-2)}{8-3x} \cdot \frac{3}{2(x-2)}=\frac{12}{8-3x}\).
As \(x \to 2\), \(u \to 0\) and \(\frac{12}{8-3x} \to \frac{12}{2}=6\), so \(\lim_{x \to 2}f(x)=e^{6}\).
For continuity at \(x=2\) we need \(k=\lim_{x \to 2}f(x)\).
\(\therefore\) \(k=e^{6}\).

Since \(45^x=9^x \cdot 5^x\), the numerator factorises:
\(45^x-9^x-5^x+1=9^x \cdot 5^x-9^x-5^x+1=(9^x-1)(5^x-1)\).
Divide numerator and denominator by \(x^2\) and use \(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{a^x-1}{x}=\log a\):
\(\lim_{x \to 0}f(x)=\frac{\log 9 \cdot \log 5}{\log k \cdot \log 3}=\frac{2\log 3 \cdot \log 5}{\log k \cdot \log 3}=\frac{2\log 5}{\log k}\).
Continuity at \(x=0\) requires this to equal \(f(0)=\frac{2}{3}\):
\(\frac{2\log 5}{\log k}=\frac{2}{3} \Rightarrow \log k=3\log 5=\log 125\).
\(\therefore\) \(k=125\).

Continuity at \(x=0\) needs \(\lim_{x \to 0^{-}}f(x)=f(0)=\lim_{x \to 0^{+}}f(x)\).
Left limit: divide numerator and denominator by \(x\) and use \(\frac{\tan x}{x} \to 1\), \(\frac{\sin x}{x} \to 1\), \(\frac{a^x-1}{x} \to \log a\):
\(\lim_{x \to 0^{-}}\frac{4\tan x+5\sin x}{a^x-1}=\frac{4+5}{\log a}=\frac{9}{\log a}\).
Right limit: \(\frac{11x+7x\cos x}{b^x-1}=\frac{x(11+7\cos x)}{b^x-1}\), so
\(\lim_{x \to 0^{+}}f(x)=\frac{11+7(1)}{\log b}=\frac{18}{\log b}\).
Equate each to \(f(0)=\frac{9}{\log 2}\):
\(\frac{9}{\log a}=\frac{9}{\log 2} \Rightarrow \log a=\log 2 \Rightarrow a=2\);
\(\frac{18}{\log b}=\frac{9}{\log 2} \Rightarrow \log b=2\log 2=\log 4 \Rightarrow b=4\).
\(\therefore\) \(a=2\) and \(b=4\).

\(|2x-3| \ge 2\) gives \(2x-3 \ge 2\) or \(2x-3 \le -2\), i.e. \(x \ge \frac{5}{2}\) or \(x \le \frac{1}{2}\). So the junctions are \(x=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(x=\frac{5}{2}\), where the quadratic branch must match \(3x+2\).
At \(x=\frac{1}{2}\): \(\frac{a}{4}+\frac{b}{2}+1=\frac{3}{2}+2=\frac{7}{2}\), so \(a+2b=10\).
At \(x=\frac{5}{2}\): \(\frac{25a}{4}+\frac{5b}{2}+1=\frac{15}{2}+2=\frac{19}{2}\), so \(25a+10b=34\).
From the first, \(a=10-2b\); substituting, \(25(10-2b)+10b=34 \Rightarrow 250-40b=34 \Rightarrow b=\frac{27}{5}\), and then \(a=10-\frac{54}{5}=-\frac{4}{5}\).
\(\therefore\) \(a=-\frac{4}{5}\) and \(b=\frac{27}{5}\).

For continuity at \(x=1\) we need \(f(1)=\lim_{x \to 1}f(x)\).
Put \(t=1-x\), so \(t \to 0\), and \(\cos \pi x=\cos(\pi-\pi t)=-\cos \pi t\). Hence
\(1+\cos \pi x=1-\cos \pi t=2\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi t}{2}\right)\), and
\(\lim_{x \to 1}\frac{1+\cos \pi x}{\pi(1-x)^2}=\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{2\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi t}{2}\right)}{\pi t^2}=\frac{2}{\pi} \cdot \frac{\pi^2}{4}\lim_{t \to 0}\left(\frac{\sin\frac{\pi t}{2}}{\frac{\pi t}{2}}\right)^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\).
\(\therefore\) \(f(1)=\frac{\pi}{2}\).

For continuity at \(x=\pi\) we need \(f(\pi)=\lim_{x \to \pi}f(x)\).
Put \(t=x-\pi\), so \(t \to 0\), and use \(1-\cos 7t=2\sin^2\left(\frac{7t}{2}\right)\):
\(\lim_{x \to \pi}\frac{1-\cos[7(x-\pi)]}{5(x-\pi)^2}=\lim_{t \to 0}\frac{2\sin^2\left(\frac{7t}{2}\right)}{5t^2}=\frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{49}{4}\lim_{t \to 0}\left(\frac{\sin\frac{7t}{2}}{\frac{7t}{2}}\right)^2=\frac{49}{10}\).
\(\therefore\) \(f(\pi)=\frac{49}{10}\).

Let \(f(x)=5^x-6x\). The exponential \(5^x\) and the polynomial \(6x\) are continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\), so \(f\) is continuous on \([1,2]\).
\(f(1)=5^1-6(1)=5-6=-1<0\) and \(f(2)=5^2-6(2)=25-12=13>0\).
So \(f(1)\) and \(f(2)\) have opposite signs, i.e. \(f(1)<0<f(2)\). By the Intermediate Value Theorem \(f\) takes every value between \(-1\) and \(13\) on \([1,2]\), in particular the value \(0\); hence there exists \(c \in (1,2)\) with \(f(c)=0\).
\(\therefore\) \(5^x-6x=0\) has a root in \([1,2]\).

Let \(f(x)=x^3-5x^2+3x+6\), a polynomial, hence continuous on \([1,5]\).
\(f(2)=8-20+6+6=0\), so \(x=2\) is itself a root lying between \(1\) and \(5\).
Next, \(f(3)=27-45+9+6=-3<0\) and \(f(4)=64-80+12+6=2>0\). Since \(f\) is continuous on \([3,4]\) and \(f(3)<0<f(4)\), the Intermediate Value Theorem gives a \(c \in (3,4)\) with \(f(c)=0\).
The two roots \(x=2\) and \(x=c \in (3,4)\) are distinct and both lie in \((1,5)\).
\(\therefore\) \(x^3-5x^2+3x+6=0\) has at least two real roots between \(x=1\) and \(x=5\).
_note: Agrees with the printed key, which reads "f(z) = 0; f(3)<0 and f(4)>0". The "f(z)" is a misprint for f(2) — f(2) = 8 - 20 + 6 + 6 = 0 exactly, and no other letter makes the key coherent. Answer-key typo only; the mathematics is right.
